title: Alice Osceola Bunn Martinez
summary: Alice Osceola Bunn Martinez (1901–1992) was a Shinnecock craftworker, trading-post founder, family historian, and oral-history contributor.
content:
Alice Osceola Bunn Martinez (January 30, 1901–January 2, 1992) was a Shinnecock craftworker, trading-post founder, family historian, and oral-history contributor. Her surviving record connects education, intergenerational craft knowledge, Native-owned commerce, and the preservation of Shinnecock community memory.1

Shinnecock family and education

Stone identifies Alice as the daughter of Maria Alice Smith and Charles Sumner Bunn and says she was born on the Shinnecock Reservation in 1901. She graduated from Southampton Public School and attended Hampton Institute. She later married Hampton Institute graduate Charles Martinez, whom Stone identifies as Chiricahua Apache. The selected sources do not give an exact marriage date.2

Craft knowledge

Alice learned matmaking from Joshua Kellis while she was young. Stone records that the mats used meadow grass whipped together with reed and that they were sold to tourists and other visitors. This account places Alice within a local chain of teaching, material knowledge, and Native craft economies rather than treating the objects as anonymous souvenirs.3

The Martinez trading post

In 1939, Alice opened what Stone describes as Long Island's first Indian trading post, beginning with a roadside teepee. After a twelve-year stay in Oklahoma, she returned in 1953 and established the permanent trading post. Stone says the Martinez family produced the beadwork, handicraft, and wood carving sold there. The source establishes the years but not exact months, so the chronology keeps both dates at year level.4

Family history and oral record

Alice's recollections preserve important details about her father Charles Sumner Bunn's work as a guide and decoy carver. Stone identifies her as the source of that account, and Nancy Shoemaker notes oral histories conducted with Alice during the 1980s. Her contribution therefore belongs not only to craft and commerce, but also to the record through which later readers encounter Shinnecock family and working life.5

A circa-1934 community record

A circa-1934 photograph caption places Alice and Charles Martinez at Conscience Point with Eugene Cuffee, Charles Bunn, Elliot Kellis, David Martinez, Anthony Beaman, and Marjorie Martinez. The caption supports the names, place, and approximate date only; it does not identify the gathering as a pageant or assign ages, clothing, performance roles, or motives to the people shown.6

Reading the map

The map chronology uses broad public places for Alice's Shinnecock birth and trading-post work and acknowledges the existing Conscience Point record. Its connecting line orders source-based records; it is not a reconstruction of her private or exact travel route.

References

  • Shinnecock Ancestors Registry, p. 19.
  • Gaynell Stone, ed., The Shinnecock Indians: A Culture History, vol. VI (1983), pp. 12, 291, 297, and 351.
  • Nancy Shoemaker, Living with Whales, p. 181.
  • John A. Strong, We Are Still Here, p. 59.
why_this_matters: Alice Bunn Martinez's record shows how craft knowledge, Native-owned commerce, education, and oral history could reinforce one another. Her work helped sustain a family economy while preserving details of Shinnecock working life that later histories might otherwise have lost.
activity_update_summary: Added a source-supported biography of Shinnecock craftworker, trading-post founder, family historian, and oral-history contributor Alice Osceola Bunn Martinez with three distinct Historic Moments.
